sections.title: Explanation
sections.body:
> **In one line:** A quorum is the minimum number of nodes that must participate in a distributed operation (read or write) for it to succeed; the cardinal rule `R + W > N` guarantees that every read overlaps a recent write, so the system can tune consistency versus availability by choosing `R` and `W` per workload.

A quorum is the engineering answer to a simple question: when data lives on `N` replicas, how many of those replicas must acknowledge a write before the coordinator calls it committed, and how many must respond to a read before the coordinator returns a value? The answer is captured in two numbers — `W`, the write quorum, and `R`, the read quorum. The fundamental invariant is `R + W > N`: any read set and any write set must overlap by at least one node, so the read is guaranteed to see the most recent write. If `R + W ≤ N`, a read can hit a set of replicas that the last write never touched, and the system silently returns stale data. This single inequality is the load-bearing wall of quorum systems, and every tunable consistency level in production — Cassandra's `QUORUM`, DynamoDB's `STRONGLY_CONSISTENT`, MongoDB's `majority` read concern — derives from it.

The power of quorums is that they expose consistency as a dial. With `N=3`, a strict quorum of `W=2, R=2` survives one node failure while still guaranteeing strong consistency, because any read intersects any write at one node. With `W=1, R=1`, you get the lowest latency and the highest availability but no consistency guarantee — a write to node A and a read from node C that never received the write return different values. With `W=N, R=1`, every read is fast and guaranteed fresh, but any node failure blocks writes — appropriate for read-heavy metadata where writes are rare and authoritative. With `W=1, R=N`, writes are fast but reads must touch every replica, suitable for write-heavy telemetry where reads are analytical and can afford the cost. The architect's job is to profile the workload's read/write ratio, latency budget, and consistency requirement, then pick the `R` and `W` that maximize throughput subject to the `R + W > N` invariant.

Real-world deployments refine this basic model. Cassandra extends quorums with rack and data-center awareness: `LOCAL_QUORUM` requires a quorum only within the local data center, accepting cross-region staleness in exchange for sub-millisecond regional latency. DynamoDB exposes `STRONGLY_CONSISTENT` reads (`R = N`) for billing and inventory records, and `EVENTUAL` reads (`R = 1`) for product reviews and recommendation feeds — the same table can serve both, on a per-request basis. Spanner and CockroachDB use quorums of Paxos groups (typically 3 or 5 nodes per group) and use 2PC across groups for cross-key transactions, building a global strongly-consistent store out of per-shard quorums.

The trade-off is fundamental and inescapable: every increment to `W` or `R` costs latency (more round trips) and availability (more nodes that must be alive). Quorums also do not eliminate the split-brain problem by themselves — if the network partitions and one side has `⌊N/2⌋` nodes, that side cannot reach quorum and must refuse writes, which is the correct behavior but means the system becomes unavailable on the smaller side. Production systems combine quorums with leader epochs, fencing tokens, and lease revocation to ensure that even when a partition heals, the minority side's stale writes cannot silently overwrite the majority's newer writes. The takeaway is that quorums are not a protocol but a contract: by choosing `R` and `W`, the system commits to a specific point on the consistency-availability-latency frontier, and the architect must understand that contract to choose the right point for each workload.

A final subtlety: quorums guarantee strong consistency only for the values that were quorum-committed. Reads still must compare versions and pick the latest, typically via timestamps or vector clocks, because the overlapping node may be the slowest to acknowledge and the coordinator may need to read several replicas to find the freshest one. This is why Cassandra's `QUORUM` read still does read-repair: it reads from a quorum, picks the highest-timestamp value, returns it, and writes it back to the laggards in the background. The quorum makes the read correct; the read-repair makes the system self-healing. Together they form a complete, tunable replication strategy that has powered everything from Amazon's shopping cart to Netflix's viewing history, and remains the workhorse of distributed data systems.

W=2| R1 C -->|ack| R2 C -.->|timeout, slow| R3 C2[Client Reader] -->|read R=2| R1 C2 -->|read R=2| R3 R1 -.->|compare ts, pick v=2| C2 R3 -.->|stale v=1, repair| R3 style R1 fill:#9f9 style R2 fill:#9f9 style R3 fill:#f99 ``` ### ASCII Diagram ``` +-----+ write x=2 (ts=10), W=2 +-----+ client --|R1 OK|<----------------------------|coord| +-----+ +-----+ +-----+ ack | client --|R2 OK|<--------------------------------| +-----+ | +-----+ timeout, slow | |R3 ..|<................................+ (no ack, write still commits) +-----+ R + W = 2 + 2 = 4 > N = 3 -> STRONG later: +-----+ read R=2 +-----+ reader --|R1 v=2|<-----------|coord|-----> returns v=2 (freshest) +-----+ +-----+ +-----+ | reader --|R3 v=1|<.............+ (stale, repaired in background) +-----+ ``` ### Walkthrough 1. Client writes `x=2` with timestamp `ts=10`; coordinator contacts all 3 replicas but waits only for `W=2` acks. R1 and R2 ack; R3 is slow. Write commits. 2. Reader issues a read with `R=2`; coordinator contacts 2 replicas (R1 and R3) and waits for both. R1 returns `v=2, ts=10`; R3 returns `v=1, ts=5` (stale). 3. Coordinator picks the freshest (`v=2`) and returns it to the reader. It also writes `v=2` back to R3 in the background (read-repair), converging the cluster.

sections.title: Code
sections.body:
```python
import random, time

class QuorumKV:
    """Tiny quorum-based KV store with tunable R and W."""
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n
        self.stores = [{"data": {}, "down": False} for _ in range(n)]

    def write(self, key, value, w):
        ts = time.time()                       # logical timestamp = write order
        acks, responses = 0, []
        for i, s in enumerate(self.stores):
            if s["down"]:
                continue
            s["data"][key] = (value, ts)       # store (value, ts) per replica
            responses.append(i)
            acks += 1
            if acks >= w:
                break                          # write quorum reached
        ok = acks >= w
        print(f"  WRITE {key}={value} (ts={ts:.3f}) acks={acks}/{self.n} "
              f"replicas={responses} -> {'COMMITTED' if ok else 'FAILED'}")
        return ok, ts

    def read(self, key, r):
        vals, contacted = [], []
        for i, s in enumerate(self.stores):
            if s["down"]:
                continue
            if key in s["data"]:
                vals.append(s["data"][key])    # (value, ts)
            contacted.append(i)
            if len(contacted) >= r:
                break                          # read quorum reached
        if len(contacted) < r:                 # not enough replicas reachable
            print(f"  READ {key} contacted={len(contacted)}/{r} -> FAILED (not enough replicas up)")
            return None
        if not vals:                            # quorum reached but key absent everywhere
            print(f"  READ {key} contacted={len(contacted)}/{r} -> MISS (key not found)")
            return None
        # Pick the freshest value, then read-repair lagging replicas.
        freshest = max(vals, key=lambda v: v[1])
        for i in contacted:
            if self.stores[i]["data"].get(key, (None, -1))[1] < freshest[1]:
                self.stores[i]["data"][key] = freshest
                print(f"    read-repair -> replica {i}")
        print(f"  READ {key} contacted={len(contacted)}/{r} -> {freshest[0]} (ts={freshest[1]:.3f})")
        return freshest[0]

# N=3, strong: R=2, W=2  (R+W=4 > 3)
kv = QuorumKV(3)
kv.write("user:42", "alice", w=2)
kv.read("user:42", r=2)

# Simulate a partitioned replica
kv.stores[2]["down"] = True
print("\n-- replica 2 down --")
kv.write("user:42", "bob", w=2)               # still quorum (1,2 down? no: 0,1 up)
kv.read("user:42", r=2)                       # reads from 0,1 -> bob

# Read-heavy tuning: W=1, R=3  (read all, write once)
print("\n-- W=1, R=3 (read-heavy) --")
kv.stores[2]["down"] = False
kv.write("hits:7", 1001, w=1)                 # write to first up replica only
kv.read("hits:7", r=3)                        # reads all -> triggers repair
```

options: This is a read-heavy, hot-key workload with low staleness tolerance (players want to see the current top 10) but not strict consistency (a 1-second-stale leader-board is…

The invariant is R + W > N, where N is the replication factor, R is the read quorum, and W is the write quorum.
quiz.explanation: The invariant is R + W > N, where N is the replication factor, R is the read quorum, and W is the write quorum. The proof is a pigeonhole argument: any set of W replicas that acknowledged the write and any set of R replicas that served the read must intersect in at least R + W - N ≥ 1 replica.

A strict quorum requires the literal R or W replicas from the replica set assigned to a key — N=3, W=2 means two of the three specific replicas that own the key.
quiz.explanation: A strict quorum requires the literal R or W replicas from the replica set assigned to a key — N=3, W=2 means two of the three specific replicas that own the key. It is correct but fragile: if two of the three are down, writes fail even though the cluster has spare capacity.

quiz.question: Why does a quorum system become unavailable when a partition leaves the minority side unable to reach quorum?
options: Odd-sized quorums tolerate the same number of failures with one fewer node, which is the dominant cost in production.
DynamoDB replicates each item across three facilities (AZs) within a region.
Cassandra exposes consistency as a per-request choice rather than a per-table choice.
The CAP theorem guarantees that during a partition a system must choose between consistency and availability.
quiz.explanation: The CAP theorem guarantees that during a partition a system must choose between consistency and availability. A quorum system chooses consistency: writes require W > N/2 acks, so the minority partition (which has fewer than half the nodes) cannot reach quorum and must refuse writes. This is the correct, safe behavior — if both sides accepted writes, they would diverge and the merge would lose data.

quiz.explanation: Read-repair is the lazy convergence mechanism layered on top of quorum reads: when a coordinator reads from R replicas, it compares versions, picks the freshest, and asynchronously writes the freshest value back to the lagging replicas. It is cheap (no background scan) and self-correcting for hot keys, because hot keys are read often and repaired quickly.
